strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in VLA learning: exploiting heterogeneous robot and human-video data while transferring across embodiments. The proposed UVMC idea, a shared discrete vision-motion latent space learned with a dual-branch VQ-VAE, is a plausible and useful direction.
weaknesses: The main comparative claims are not fully supported. XR-1 benefits from a very large in-house XR-D dataset and substantial compute, while the baseline training/pretraining conditions are not specified at a level that makes the comparisons clearly fair. Some out-of-box evaluations include tasks from XR-D, so the degree of true held-out generalization is unclear.

The method description has important ambiguities. The KL alignment between q(z_mo) and q(z_vis) is underspecified, the way human-only videos become aligned to the robot motion space is not convincingly justified because they only use the visual loss, and the role of UVMC at inference appears to be auxiliary supervision rather than an explicit intermediate control representation. There are also notation errors, such as concatenating the motion code with itself in the UVMC definition.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper provides useful high-level hyperparameters, dataset sizes, and GPU-hour estimates, but relies heavily on private XR-D data, real-robot infrastructure, and unspecified implementation details. There is no clear code/model/data release plan, and success evaluation by human raters lacks details on criteria, inter-rater reliability, or statistical uncertainty.

The experimental scale is impressive, but the analysis does not include confidence intervals or statistical tests despite using 20 rollouts per task. Many tables report large success-rate differences, but without uncertainty it is hard to judge robustness, especially for tasks with high variance.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics/safety discussion. This is a material omission for a real-world robotic foundation model trained with human videos and deployed across varied manipulation settings.

Presentation is uneven. The manuscript is readable at a high level and contains many figures/tables, but there are numerous typos, notation inconsistencies, formatting issues in large tables, and over-strong causal language that exceeds the evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable VLA learning across heterogeneous robot embodiments, human videos, and robotic datasets.
The empirical scope is ambitious, with reported real-world evaluations over six robot embodiments, more than 120 tasks, and over 14,000 rollouts.

The proposed UVMC idea, a shared discrete latent space for visual dynamics and robot motion, is a reasonable and potentially useful direction for injecting structured intermediate supervision into VLA training.
The appendices provide some useful implementation details, including model sizes, training steps, compute estimates, dataset composition, and task descriptions.
weaknesses: The central claims are not convincingly supported because the evaluation appears seriously confounded by data and training differences. XR-1 uses a large in-house XR-D dataset and multi-stage pretraining, while it is unclear whether baselines are given comparable pretraining data, compute, tuning, or adaptation protocols. In the out-of-box setting, baselines are described as lacking XR-D pretraining, which makes the comparison particularly hard to interpret.

The method description has important ambiguities and inconsistencies. For example, the paper says UVMC concatenates motion codes and visual dynamics codes but writes the motion code twice; Stage-2 uses MSE to predict codes despite the representation being discrete; and the KL alignment between latent code distributions is underspecified. These issues make it difficult to understand or reproduce the actual algorithm.

The claimed benefit from human demonstrations is weakly evidenced. Human videos only optimize the visual reconstruction loss, so the paper does not clearly show how actionless human data become motor-grounded beyond an indirect assertion. There is no focused ablation isolating Ego4D or human-video contribution.

The ablations are too limited relative to the claims. They cover only a small subset of tasks and do not isolate several key factors, such as shared codebook vs separate codebooks, visual-only vs motion-only codes, human-video data, dataset mixture weights, model scale, and fair compute/data-matched baselines.

Statistical reliability is underdeveloped. Results use 20 rollouts per task and human success judgments, but the paper reports no confidence intervals, variance across seeds or evaluators, significance tests, evaluator blinding, or detailed failure analysis.

Reproducibility is poor for an ICML main-track claim of this scale. The largest and most important dataset is in-house, no code/model release plan is clearly stated, baseline training details are sparse, and reproducing the work requires very large compute and real robot infrastructure.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. The manuscript contains many typos, formatting problems, hard-to-read tables, inconsistent terminology, and overclaimed causal explanations such as attributing baseline failures to gradient conflicts without direct evidence.

The paper lacks an adequate limitations and ethics discussion. For a large-scale real-world robotics system trained partly on human videos and deployed on physical robots, the manuscript should discuss safety, data consent/privacy, deployment risks, failure modes, and constraints on generalization.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in generalist robot learning: using heterogeneous robot and human video data to improve vision-language-action policies across embodiments. The proposed Unified Vision-Motion Codes are a plausible and useful way to align visual dynamics with motion/action representations.

The empirical scale is a major strength. The paper reports more than 14k real-world rollouts across six robot embodiments and over 120 manipulation tasks, with comparisons to strong contemporary VLA baselines including pi0, pi0.5, RDT, UniVLA, and GR00T-N1.5.

The results are consistently favorable across many settings: XR-1 improves average success rates on Dual-Arm UR-5e, Tien Kung 2.0, Tien Kung 1.0, Dual-Arm Franka, AgileX Cobot Magic, and Single-Arm UR-5e, and the gains are often large on difficult bimanual, contact-rich, and long-horizon tasks.

The ablations are informative. They separately examine UVMC, the cross-modal alignment loss, lightweight model instantiation, pretraining data scale, and cross-embodiment transfer, supporting the claim that the representation learning stage is not merely incidental.

The paper provides useful implementation details in the appendix, including architecture choices, codebook size, batch sizes, training steps, GPU cost, dataset composition, and task descriptions. The writing is generally clear and the high-level framework is easy to follow.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited by reliance on a large in-house dataset, proprietary or difficult-to-access robot platforms, massive compute, and real-world evaluation infrastructure. Although implementation details are provided, it is unclear whether code, XR-D, trained checkpoints, or evaluation videos will be released, making independent verification difficult.

The fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully established. The paper compares against many strong models, but gives limited detail on how each baseline was adapted, tuned, pretrained, or fine-tuned under matched data and compute budgets. Some baselines collapse to 0% on many tasks, which raises questions about implementation and tuning rather than only method superiority.

The central representation-learning formulation has some underspecified technical points. For example, the KL alignment term between visual and motion latent distributions is not fully defined for the VQ-VAE setting, and the text appears to contain a typo when concatenating motion and visual codes. More precise definitions would improve soundness.

The evidence for using human videos is weaker than the overall evaluation suggests. Ego4D is included in Stage-1, but the paper does not cleanly isolate how much human-only video contributes relative to robot data, nor does it deeply analyze whether visual codes from human demonstrations truly align with robot motion space.

The paper would benefit from statistical treatment of real-world rollout variability. Most evaluations use 20 rollouts per task and report point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or evaluator agreement details, which makes it hard to judge reliability of close comparisons.

The limitation and ethics discussion is thin. For a real-world robotics system, more discussion is needed on safety, failure modes, human evaluation protocols, deployment constraints, dataset privacy/licensing for human videos, and risks from unintended robot actions.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving VLA policies across heterogeneous robot embodiments and actionless human/video data. The proposed UVMC idea, a dual-branch VQ-VAE aligning visual dynamics and robot motion in a shared discrete latent space, is a reasonable and useful extension of prior latent-action or visual-dynamics approaches.

The empirical scope is unusually large for robotics: the manuscript reports more than 14,000 real-world rollouts over six embodiments and 120+ tasks, including bimanual, contact-rich, deformable-object, and long-horizon settings. Results are consistently strong, with XR-1 outperforming π0/π0.5, RDT, UniVLA, and GR00T-N1.5 across multiple tables.

The ablations are directionally helpful. Removing UVMC/KL alignment hurts performance, scaling Stage-1 pretraining data improves success rates monotonically, and motion-only/vision-only codes underperform combined UVMC. The lightweight XR-1-Light experiment also suggests the idea is not purely a large-model artifact.

The manuscript includes useful implementation details, dataset counts, training compute estimates, inference frequency, additional robot/task tables, simulation results on CALVIN, qualitative retrieval/t-SNE analyses, and a failure case discussion. Presentation is generally clear and the paper is easy to follow despite its breadth.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are not fully controlled. XR-1 benefits from a very large private XR-D dataset and a multi-stage training pipeline, while the exact pretraining/fine-tuning treatment of baselines is not specified with enough precision to determine whether gains come from UVMC, data scale/composition, architecture, optimization budget, or implementation quality. This is especially important because some reported baseline failures are near zero on many tasks.

Reproducibility is limited. The project URL appears blank in the abstract, XR-D/in-house demonstrations are central but not evidently released, baseline training recipes are underspecified, and the compute requirement is extremely high. Although hyperparameters are listed, an external group could not realistically reproduce the central real-world claims from the manuscript alone.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper claims embodiment-agnostic and human-video-to-action alignment, but human demonstrations only optimize the visual reconstruction objective, and the mechanism by which actionless human videos are mapped into robot action space is not directly validated beyond a small Ego4D ablation. Retrieval/t-SNE results are suggestive but not decisive evidence of causal or controllable semantic alignment.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates and statistical analysis. Most real-world numbers use 20 rollouts per task and human success judgments, but no confidence intervals, repeated seeds, inter-rater agreement, or significance tests are reported. Many task-level differences could be noisy, and aggregate averages hide task selection and variance.

The out-of-box evaluation is potentially misleading: the selected tasks are stated to come from XR-D and cover only 0.45% of that dataset, so XR-1 may have seen related or exact data during Stage-2, while baselines are fine-tuned differently. This does not cleanly establish zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks.

Methodological details around UVMC are somewhat under-specified. The KL alignment between posterior distributions over quantized codes is not defined rigorously, the use of MSE to regress discrete code embeddings in Stage-2 is only briefly described, and it is not always clear whether UVMC is used only as auxiliary training supervision or also as an inference-time conditioning signal.

Limitations and ethics are weakly treated. The paper has a short failure analysis noting precision deficiencies, but the formal impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss safety, deployment risks, teleoperation/data provenance, human-video consent considerations, or potential misuse of more capable generalist robotic policies.

strengths: Ambitious real-robot evaluation scale: the paper reports more than 14k rollouts over six embodiments and 120+ tasks, with detailed per-task success tables in the appendix. This is a meaningful effort in a domain where evaluation is expensive.

The core idea of learning joint discrete vision-motion codes and using them as auxiliary supervision for VLA training is plausible and relevant. The method is simple enough to be potentially useful across backbones, and the XR-1-Light experiment suggests some portability.
The paper compares against several strong contemporary VLA baselines and includes ablations for UVMC components, data scale, Ego4D usage, codebook settings, and cross-embodiment transfer.

The reported empirical gains are large across many embodiments, including unseen Tien Kung 2.0, and the paper includes useful qualitative analyses such as nearest-neighbor retrieval, t-SNE visualizations, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not sufficiently supported by a clear and reproducible evaluation protocol. The paper does not precisely specify train/test splits, whether evaluation tasks overlap with XR-D or fine-tuning demonstrations, how held-out scenes/objects are selected, or how human success labels are standardized. This is especially serious because the main evidence is real-world success rate tables.

Baseline fairness is unclear. XR-1 receives massive Stage-1 and Stage-2 pretraining on private/in-house data, including XR-D, while it is not clear that baselines receive comparable pretraining exposure, tuning budgets, hyperparameter searches, or implementations. Some claims of superiority may therefore reflect data/compute advantages rather than the proposed UVMC mechanism.

Reproducibility is weak. XR-D appears private, the project link is missing/blank, implementation details are incomplete for reproducing data processing and training, and the reported compute is very large. Without code, pretrained checkpoints, datasets, or a public benchmark protocol, others cannot reliably build on or verify the results.

The method description leaves important technical ambiguities. The KL alignment loss is defined over q(z) in codebook space, but the posterior distribution for nearest-neighbor VQ codes is not clearly specified. The claim that human-only demonstrations can be mapped effectively into robot action space is not directly validated beyond a small Ego4D ablation.

The ablations do not isolate the contribution convincingly enough. Many comparisons conflate UVMC, pretraining scale, XR-D pretraining, model capacity, and downstream fine-tuning. The strongest evidence for UVMC is on six tasks, while the headline claims span more than 120 tasks.

Statistical rigor is limited. The paper reports 20 rollouts per task but gives no confidence intervals, significance tests, variance over seeds, inter-rater agreement for human evaluation, or failure-rate uncertainty. Given many success rates differ by 5-10 points, this matters.

Presentation is polished at a high level but often overclaims causal explanations, e.g. attributing baseline failures to optimization collapse or conflicting gradients based mostly on qualitative rollout observations rather than direct optimization evidence.

The ethics/impact statement is boilerplate and inadequate for a real-world robotics system trained on large-scale human and robot video data. Safety, deployment risks, privacy/licensing of video data, labor/teleoperation concerns, and misuse risks are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in VLA robotics: learning transferable low-level control from heterogeneous robot and human video data. The proposed UVMC representation, learned with a dual-branch VQ-VAE over visual dynamics and robot motion, is a plausible and useful mechanism for injecting structured supervision into VLA policies.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for real-world robot learning: more than 14k rollouts, six embodiments, 123 tasks, and comparisons against strong recent baselines including pi0.5, pi0, RDT, UniVLA, and GR00T-N1.5. XR-1 shows consistent gains across Dual-Arm UR-5e, Tien Kung 1.0/2.0, Dual-Arm Franka, AgileX Cobot Magic, and Single-Arm UR-5e.

The ablations are meaningful and support the main design choices. The paper studies UVMC versus no UVMC, KL alignment, data scaling, codebook size/dimension, motion-only versus vision-only codes, Ego4D contribution, and cross-embodiment transfer. These results make the central claim more convincing than a single leaderboard-style comparison would.

The paper provides useful implementation detail in the appendix, including model sizes, codebook settings, batch sizes, learning rates, training steps, action horizon, compute costs, and inference rates. This improves technical transparency, even though full reproducibility remains difficult.

The work has clear practical significance. The reported gains are especially compelling on harder bimanual, long-horizon, deformable, and contact-rich tasks where several baselines collapse to near-zero success. The out-of-box and fast-adaptation experiments also strengthen the case that the learned representation is useful beyond standard fine-tuning.

Presentation is generally strong: the paper is well structured, the motivation is clear, and the main figures/tables communicate the experimental story effectively. The appendix adds substantial detail rather than only peripheral material.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is still limited by the dependence on large in-house datasets, proprietary or difficult-to-access robot platforms, and very high pretraining compute. The manuscript lists many dataset statistics and hyperparameters, but it is unclear whether code, trained checkpoints, full evaluation videos, task definitions, and XR-D data will be released in a form sufficient for independent verification. The project link in the abstract appears incomplete.

The evaluation relies on human-judged success rates with 20 rollouts per task, but the paper does not report confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement, random seeds, trial ordering, or statistical tests. Given the high variance of real-world robotics, some per-task differences may be noisy even though the aggregate trend is strong.

Baseline fairness is not fully resolved. The paper notes implementation choices for pi0 and compares against several strong systems, but it is not always clear that all baselines receive equally optimized hyperparameters, comparable pretraining exposure, and equivalent adaptation budgets. The out-of-box setting is also somewhat asymmetric because XR-1 uses XR-D pretraining while baselines without XR-D are fine-tuned on selected tasks.

Some mechanistic claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. t-SNE visualizations and nearest-neighbor retrieval are suggestive, but they do not by themselves prove embodiment-invariant or causal vision-motion representations. Phrases such as mapping human-only demonstrations into the robot action space and reducing conflicting gradients would benefit from more direct quantitative diagnostics.

The method section leaves some ambiguity around the alignment loss and discrete-code prediction. For example, q over codebook space is not fully specified, and the interaction between concatenated vision/motion codes, learnable tokens, and action-head training could be described more precisely for reimplementation.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The appendix includes failure cases, especially precision failures on small objects and bimanual coordination, but there is little discussion of safety during deployment, human video privacy/licensing, labor/data collection conditions, or the risks of real-world robotic manipulation errors.

The contribution is technically solid but partly incremental in its ingredients: VQ-VAE tokenization, latent action/visual dynamics pretraining, and VLA fine-tuning are all established directions. The originality lies in the unified vision-motion code and scale of validation rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.
